question.text: Why does a Cat III AIF's convertible arbitrage strategy incur a 'borrowing fee' for short equity positions?

answer.text: The fund must borrow the shares to short and pays a borrowing fee; dividends declared during the short period are also forgone by the short-position investor.
SEBI levies a short-sale tax on Cat III AIFs.
It is a penalty for exceeding 2x leverage.
It is a fee paid to the Acquirer in a merger deal.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Section 10.1.3 (Example 10.6), the fund pays a borrowing fee to borrow shares needed for the short position, and dividends declared during the short period do not accrue to the short-position investor. The Trap: Option B invents a SEBI short-sale tax. Option C mis-frames the borrow fee as a penalty for leverage breach. Option D is unrelated merger-deal terminology. Note: Borrowing fees and dividends forgone are the two source-backed economic costs of the short leg in Cat III convertible arbitrage.
